solver.kind: blind AI solver (separate agent, answer-free packet, rubric v2)

Q077-01.notes: 700% greater => 8x initial; 2^(t/5)=8 => t=15. Distractors: 14 (2^(t/5)=7 -> t~14.04, the 'percent = multiple' trap), 3, 40 (8*5).

flags: minor: direct calculator substitution of t=2 and t=5 settles it immediately; D matches two of three points (good distractor).

Q077-03.notes: x^2+6x+4=(x+3)^2-5 -> 3 left, 5 down. Graphing vertex (-3,-5) also works.

Q077-06.notes: g(f(x))=sqrt(x^2)=|x|, equals x iff x>=0. Domain of composition is all reals (x^2>=0), so D is the trap; A/C come from misused domain restrictions.

Q077-07.notes: OP=10; half-chord = altitude of right triangle OAP to hypotenuse = 6*8/10=4.8; AB=9.6. Distractors 4.8 (half), 7.2 (36/5), 12.8 (64/5) are all natural segment lengths.

flags: minor: the 15 m spacing cancels (h = 6*9/(6+9) regardless of distance); fine as given setup but it is not actually needed.
minor: well-known classic 'crossed wires/poles' puzzle (harmonic-mean result), recognizable to some students; not a known official SAT item.

Q077-09.notes: Inscribed angle CAB=25 -> central angle COB=50; OC perpendicular to tangent CD; in triangle OCD angle ODC=180-90-50=40, and since D is beyond B, angle ADC=angle ODC=40.

Q077-10.notes: Half-height 4, sphere radius 5 -> cylinder radius 3; V=pi*9*8=72pi. 200pi uses r=5.

Q077-11.notes: cos(90-x)=sin x=0.6; height=50 sin x=30. D (40) is the cos trap.

Q077-12.notes: AC=6/cos30=4sqrt3; triangle ACD is isosceles right at C so AD=AC*sqrt2=4sqrt6. B is AC, A is BC.

flags: minor: classic square-with-equilateral-triangle configuration, familiar from competition practice.
Q077-13.notes: AP=AD, angle PAD=30 -> angle ADP=75 -> angle PDC=90-75=15. Coordinates confirm.

flags: minor: the 64 degree value is irrelevant (bisectors of same-side interior angles always meet at 90), so a student may guess 90 without computing; arguably over-determined/red-herring data.
Q077-14.notes: Same-side interior angles 64 and 116; halves 32+58=90; angle APB=180-90=90.
